lead: Ogden climbs from old railroad neighborhoods up to the benches below the Wasatch. Old basements, cold winters and spring runoff from the canyons drive its water damage.
risk: frozen pipes, old basements and spring snowmelt runoff
why: Ogden grew as a railroad town, and it shows in its housing. About 19% of homes were built before 1940, and nearly two-thirds before 1980. Many of the older houses near downtown and Historic 25th Street have stone or brick basements and original drain lines. Those basements seep after heavy rain and snowmelt, and old clay sewers crack and fill with roots.

Winters bring hard freezes and inversions that keep cold air trapped for days. Pipes in basements, crawl spaces and outside walls can freeze and burst, often while a family is away. In big snow years, spring melt pours out of Ogden Canyon and the smaller canyons above the East Bench. Runoff can flood yards and push water toward basement window wells.
image_alt: Small brick house with snow on the roof and steps
image_caption: Long cold snaps in Ogden can freeze and split pipes in basements and walls.
tips: Keep the heat on and cabinet doors open during long cold snaps.
Shut off and drain outdoor faucets each fall.
Add window well covers on the bench before spring melt.
Have an old sewer line scoped and roots cleared.
areas: Calls come from Downtown Ogden, Historic 25th Street, the East Bench, Jefferson, Mount Ogden and the Central Bench, plus North Ogden, South Ogden, Roy and Riverdale.

faq.q: How do I keep pipes from freezing in my older Ogden home?
faq.a: Keep the heat at 55°F or higher, even when you travel. Insulate pipes in basements, crawl spaces and outside walls, and open cabinet doors on very cold nights. Shut off and drain outdoor faucets in fall. Know where your main shutoff is in case a pipe bursts.
